name: Basel I minimum Tier 1 capital ratio
prompt: Under Basel I, what minimum ratio must core (Tier 1) capital bear to risk-weighted assets?

variables.meaning: core capital: equity (less goodwill) and noncumulative perpetual preferred stock
risk-weighted assets: each asset (or credit equivalent amount) times its risk weight

corruptions.why: 8% is the floor for total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2); the Tier 1 floor is 4%.
Basel I scales capital by risk-weighted assets, not by unweighted total assets.

intuition: Half of the 8% must be the good stuff: at least 4% of RWA in core Tier 1 capital.

name: Basel I minimum total capital ratio
prompt: Under Basel I, what minimum ratio must total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) bear to risk-weighted assets?

variables.meaning: Tier 1 plus Tier 2 capital
risk-weighted assets: each asset (or credit equivalent amount) times its risk weight

corruptions.why: 4% is the Tier 1 floor; total capital must be at least 8% of RWA.
The 8% applies to risk-weighted assets, not to the unweighted balance sheet.

intuition: The famous Basel 8%: capital of 8 cents per risk-weighted dollar, which is why RWA = 12.5 x capital.

name: Original Exposure Method add-on: interest rate contracts over two years
prompt: Under Basel I's Original Exposure Method, what add-on factor D applies to an interest rate contract with maturity M greater than two years?

variables.meaning: add-on factor, as a percentage of notional principal
maturity of the contract in years (greater than two)
the closest integer to X

corruptions.why: 5% + 3% per year is the foreign exchange schedule; interest rate contracts use 1% + 1% per year.
The increment counts years beyond the first, INT[M-1], so a 3-year contract gets 1% + 2% = 3%, not 4%.

sensitivities.why: Each additional year of maturity adds another 1% of notional to the add-on.

intuition: Interest rate add-on: start at 1% and add 1% for every year past the first.

name: Original Exposure Method add-on: foreign exchange contracts over two years
prompt: Under Basel I's Original Exposure Method, what add-on factor D applies to a foreign exchange contract with maturity M greater than two years?

variables.meaning: add-on factor, as a percentage of notional principal
maturity of the contract in years (greater than two)
the closest integer to X

corruptions.why: 1% + 1% per year is the interest rate schedule; FX contracts carry the larger 5% + 3% per year.
The increment counts years beyond the first, INT[M-1], not the full maturity.

sensitivities.why: Each additional year of maturity adds another 3% of notional to the add-on.

intuition: FX add-ons are steeper than rate add-ons: start at 5% and add 3% per year past the first.

name: Credit equivalent amount with netting (1995 amendment)
prompt: After the 1995 amendment, how is the credit equivalent amount of a netting set of derivatives computed from the contract values, their add-ons and the net replacement ratio?

variables.meaning: credit equivalent amount of the netted derivatives portfolio
current market value of contract i (positive = asset to the bank)
number of contracts in the netting set
add-on amount for contract j (add-on factor times notional), for potential future changes in value
net replacement ratio: current exposure with netting compared with current exposure without netting

corruptions.why: The fixed part is 40% of the add-on and the netting-sensitive part is 60%; swapping them gives too little credit for netting.
Flooring each contract at zero before summing is the no-netting exposure; with netting the values are summed first and only the net is floored.
Only 60% of the add-on is scaled by NRR; the other 40% of the add-on is always charged in full, however good the netting.

sensitivities.why: A higher NRR means netting helps less, so more of the add-on survives into the CEA.
Bigger add-ons for potential future exposure raise the CEA.
Raises the CEA only while the net sum of values is positive; below zero the max floor holds the first term at zero.

intuition: Net the values first and floor at zero; then keep 40% of the add-on regardless and let netting (NRR) shrink the other 60%.

name: Total capital under the 1996 amendment (credit + market risk)
prompt: Before Basel II, how was a bank's total required capital computed from its credit risk and market risk RWA?

variables.meaning: required regulatory capital (only credit and market risk were charged)
risk-weighted assets for credit risk, on- plus off-balance sheet
market risk capital charge grossed up by 12.5

corruptions.why: 12.5 converts capital into RWA; going from RWA to capital you multiply by 8%.

corruptions.latex: \text{total capital}=0.08\times(\text{credit risk RWA}+\text{market risk RWA}+\text{operational risk RWA})
corruptions.why: Operational risk capital only arrived with Basel II; before then only credit and market risk were charged.
4% is the Tier 1 minimum; total capital is 8% of RWA.

sensitivities.why: Each dollar of credit RWA needs 8 cents of capital.
Each dollar of market RWA needs 8 cents of capital.

intuition: Add the two RWA buckets and take 8%; operational risk isn't in the sum until Basel II.

name: Market risk RWA under the internal models approach (1996)
prompt: Under the 1996 amendment, how are market risk RWA computed from yesterday's VaR, the average VaR and the multiplier?

variables.meaning: risk-weighted assets for market risk
previous day's market risk VaR (internal models: typically 10-day, 99%)
average VaR over the preceding 60 trading days
multiplicative factor (3 in the notes' example), adjusted according to the number of backtesting exceptions

corruptions.why: The multiplier scales the 60-day average VaR, not yesterday's VaR.
It is the larger of the two that is charged, not the smaller.
The bracket is the capital charge; RWA is that charge times 12.5 (= 1/0.08), not times 0.08.

sensitivities.why: Raises RWA only when m x average VaR is the binding term in the max; otherwise no effect.
Raises RWA only when m x average VaR exceeds yesterday's VaR.
Raises RWA only when yesterday's VaR exceeds m x average VaR.

intuition: Capital is the worse of yesterday's VaR and the multiplied 60-day average; times 12.5 turns that charge into RWA.

name: Credit risk RWA: on- plus off-balance sheet
prompt: How is total credit risk RWA assembled from the bank's on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet exposures?

variables.meaning: total risk-weighted assets for credit risk
each on-balance-sheet asset times its risk weight
each off-balance-sheet item's credit equivalent amount times the counterparty risk weight

corruptions.why: Off-balance-sheet items (guarantees, letters of credit, swaps) also attract credit RWA via their credit equivalent amounts.
Off-balance-sheet notionals are first converted to credit equivalent amounts and then risk-weighted; the raw notional is not RWA.

sensitivities.why: More risk-weighted loans and securities add one-for-one.
More risk-weighted off-balance-sheet exposure adds one-for-one.

intuition: Credit RWA covers both sides of the line: weighted assets plus weighted credit equivalents of off-balance-sheet items.

name: IRB capital as stressed loss minus expected loss (Formula 1)
prompt: Under Basel II IRB, how is credit capital built from each exposure's EAD, LGD, 99.9% worst-case default rate and PD?

variables.meaning: credit risk capital (covers unexpected loss only)
exposure at default of exposure i
loss given default of exposure i (decimal)
default rate that will not be exceeded with 99.9% confidence over one year (decimal)
one-year probability of default of exposure i (decimal)

corruptions.why: Expected loss is subtracted: banks are expected to cover EL through pricing, so capital covers only unexpected loss.
Expected loss is taken off the 99.9% loss, not added to it.
LGD is already the loss fraction; 1 - LGD would be the recovery rate.

sensitivities.why: A higher worst-case default rate widens the gap over expected loss.
Holding DR99.9 fixed, a higher PD raises expected loss and so lowers capital; in practice DR99.9 rises with PD too.
LGD scales both terms; as long as DR99.9 exceeds PD, the difference grows.
More exposure scales up the unexpected loss.

intuition: Capital is the 99.9% bad-year loss minus the loss you already expect and price for: unexpected loss only.

name: IRB capital = one-year 99.9% VaR minus expected loss
prompt: Under Basel II IRB, how is credit risk capital expressed as a single tail-loss measure (at what confidence and horizon) adjusted for the losses banks already price in?

variables.meaning: IRB credit risk capital
one-year credit VaR at 99.9% confidence (the 99.9% worst-case loss)
expected loss, EAD x LGD x PD

corruptions.why: 99% over 10 days is the market risk VaR standard; IRB credit capital uses 99.9% over one year.
Expected loss is covered by pricing and is subtracted, not added.

sensitivities.why: A fatter 99.9% loss tail requires more capital.
Holding VaR fixed, more of the tail loss is already expected and priced, leaving less unexpected loss.

intuition: Capital covers the surprise, not the average: 99.9% one-year VaR less expected loss.

name: IRB capital for a single exposure with maturity adjustment (Formula 2)
prompt: Under Basel II IRB, how is capital for one exposure computed from EAD, LGD, DR99.9, PD and the maturity adjustment?

variables.meaning: IRB credit risk capital for the exposure
exposure at default
loss given default (decimal)
worst-case default rate at 99.9% confidence over one year (decimal)
probability of default (decimal)
maturity adjustment

corruptions.why: Multiplying by 12.5 gives RWA (Formula 3), not capital.
PD is subtracted so that capital covers only unexpected loss.
The maturity adjustment multiplies: longer maturities need more capital.

sensitivities.why: Capital scales with exposure.
Higher loss severity scales capital up (given DR99.9 > PD).
A worse 99.9% default rate widens unexpected loss.
A larger maturity adjustment scales capital up (given DR99.9 > PD).

intuition: Unexpected default rate (DR99.9 - PD) times loss per default (EAD x LGD), stretched by a maturity adjustment.

name: IRB maturity adjustment (MA)
prompt: In the Basel II IRB formula, how is the maturity adjustment computed from the exposure's maturity M and the parameter b?

variables.meaning: maturity adjustment
maturity of the exposure in years (fixed at 2.5 under foundation IRB)
maturity parameter, b = [0.11852 - 0.05478 ln(PD)]^2

corruptions.why: The 2.5 anchors maturity in the numerator (M - 2.5) and the 1.5 sits in the denominator; swapping them changes the value.
Upside down: longer maturity must raise MA, so (M - 2.5) belongs in the numerator.
Without the 1 - 1.5b denominator the adjustment at M = 2.5 would be 1 rather than 1/(1 - 1.5b).

sensitivities.why: b is positive, so each extra year of maturity raises the numerator.
dMA/db has the sign of (M - 1): a larger b raises MA for any maturity above one year (always at the 2.5-year benchmark) and lowers it below one year.

intuition: At the 2.5-year benchmark MA collapses to 1/(1 - 1.5b); every year beyond 2.5 adds b more on top.

name: IRB maturity parameter b
prompt: In the Basel II IRB maturity adjustment, how is the parameter b computed from the probability of default?

variables.meaning: maturity parameter used in the maturity adjustment
probability of default (decimal, floored at 0.03%)

corruptions.why: ln(PD) is negative, so it must be subtracted to push b up; with a plus sign b is tiny and not even monotone in PD.
The bracket is squared; without the square b would be about 0.50 instead of 0.247 at PD = 0.1%.
The formula uses the natural log of PD, not PD itself.

sensitivities.why: Higher PD makes ln(PD) less negative, shrinking the bracket: safer borrowers get a larger b and so a larger maturity adjustment.

intuition: Low-PD names have more to lose from time, so b (and the maturity penalty) is biggest for the safest borrowers.

name: IRB risk-weighted assets (Formula 3)
prompt: Under Basel II IRB, how are risk-weighted assets for an exposure computed from EAD, LGD, DR99.9, PD and the maturity adjustment?

variables.meaning: risk-weighted assets for the exposure (multiply by 8% to get capital)
exposure at default
loss given default (decimal)
worst-case default rate at 99.9% confidence over one year (decimal)
probability of default (decimal)
maturity adjustment

corruptions.why: The bracket is already capital; RWA grosses it up by 12.5, and you multiply RWA by 8% to get back to capital.
PD (expected loss) is subtracted from DR99.9, not added.
Dropping PD would charge expected loss as well, but IRB capital covers only unexpected loss.

sensitivities.why: RWA scales with exposure.
Higher loss severity raises RWA (given DR99.9 > PD).
A higher 99.9% default rate raises unexpected loss.
A longer-maturity adjustment raises RWA.

intuition: RWA is just IRB capital times 12.5; for a high-grade loan it lands far below Basel I's 100% weight.

name: CDS expected premium payment per period
prompt: In valuing a CDS, what is the protection buyer's expected premium payment on a payment date?

variables.meaning: expected premium paid by the protection buyer on the payment date
risk-neutral probability the reference entity has survived to the payment date
CDS notional
CDS spread (annual, decimal)

corruptions.why: Premiums are paid only if the entity has survived, so they are weighted by survival, not default, probability.

corruptions.latex: \text{expected payment} = \text{probability of survival} \times (1-\text{recovery rate}) \times \text{notional principal} \times s
corruptions.why: Recovery affects the protection payoff, not the premium the buyer pays.

sensitivities.why: More likely to survive to the date means the premium is more likely to be paid.
Premium scales with notional.
A wider spread is a bigger premium.

intuition: You only pay the premium if the name is still alive: survival x notional x spread.

name: CDS expected protection payoff per period
prompt: In valuing a CDS, what is the expected payoff to the protection buyer for a period?

variables.meaning: expected protection payment to the buyer if default occurs in the period
recovery rate on the reference obligation (decimal)
risk-neutral probability of default during the period
CDS notional

corruptions.why: The seller pays the loss, i.e. the part not recovered: (1 - recovery rate).
Payoffs occur only on default, so they are weighted by PD, not survival.

sensitivities.why: Higher recovery leaves less loss for the seller to cover.
Default more likely means the payoff is more likely.
Payoff scales with notional.

intuition: Protection pays the loss (1 - R) only in default, so weight by PD.

name: CDS accrual payment on mid-period default
prompt: When default is assumed to occur mid-period, what expected accrued premium does the protection buyer owe for that period (per unit notional)?

variables.meaning: expected accrued premium owed on default, per unit of notional
probability of default during the period
annual CDS spread (decimal)

corruptions.why: Accrual is owed only when default happens mid-period, so it is weighted by PD.
Default is assumed at mid-period, so only half a year of premium has accrued.

sensitivities.why: More likely default means accrual is more likely owed.
A wider spread means more premium accrues in half a year.

intuition: Default lands halfway through the year, so the buyer owes half a year's spread, weighted by PD.

inputs.name: s
inputs.unit: decimal (use 1 for per unit of spread)

name: Survival probability from a constant hazard rate
prompt: Given a constant hazard rate, what is the probability that the reference entity survives to time t?

variables.meaning: probability of survival to time t
hazard rate (default intensity) per annum, decimal
time in years

corruptions.why: 1 - e^{-lambda t} is the cumulative default probability, the complement of survival.
Survival decays with lambda times t; dividing by t would make survival rise over time.

sensitivities.why: A higher default intensity erodes survival faster.
The longer the horizon, the lower the chance of surviving it.

intuition: Survival decays exponentially at the hazard rate: 3% hazard leaves about 97% alive after a year.

name: Unconditional default probability in year t
prompt: How is the (unconditional) probability of default during year t obtained from the survival probabilities?

variables.meaning: probability of default during year t, as seen today
probability of survival to the start of year t
probability of survival to the end of year t

corruptions.why: Survival falls over time, so this ordering gives a negative number.
1 - PS_t is the cumulative default probability to t, not the probability of default within year t.

sensitivities.why: More survivors entering the year means more can default in it.
More survivors at the end of the year means fewer defaulted during it.

intuition: Defaults in a year are the survivors lost during that year: last year's survival minus this year's.

name: CDS breakeven condition
prompt: What equality sets the fair (breakeven) CDS spread?

variables.meaning: present value of expected premium payments, including accrual payments on default
present value of the expected protection payoff

corruptions.why: The buyer is paid the loss net of recovery, not the recovery itself.
The legs are equated in present value: payments land on anniversary dates and payoffs mid-period, so each must be discounted before they are set equal.

intuition: Fair spread: what the buyer expects to pay in (premiums plus accrual) equals what they expect to get back.

name: Breakeven CDS spread s = C/(A+B)
prompt: How is the breakeven CDS spread computed from the PV of expected payments per unit spread, the PV of accrual payments per unit spread, and the PV of the expected payoff?

variables.meaning: breakeven CDS spread (decimal, per year)
PV of expected premium payments per unit of spread
PV of expected accrual payments per unit of spread
PV of the expected payoff

corruptions.why: Ignoring the accrual term B overstates the spread, because the buyer is credited with less value paid in.
The spread is payoff value per unit of premium annuity, not the other way round.
Accrual payments are additional premium flows, so they add to the annuity.

sensitivities.why: A more valuable protection leg requires a higher spread.
A larger premium annuity spreads the cost over more value paid in.
More accrual value paid in lowers the spread needed.

intuition: Spread = protection value / premium annuity, and the annuity includes the half-period accrual.

name: Mark-to-market value of a CDS to the protection seller
prompt: What is the mark-to-market value of an existing CDS to the protection seller?

variables.meaning: current value of the CDS to the seller (the buyer's value is the negative)
PV of expected premium payments the seller receives, at the contract spread
PV of the expected protection payoff the seller pays

corruptions.why: That is the buyer's mark; the seller receives premiums and pays the protection.
The payoff is an outflow for the seller and is subtracted.

sensitivities.why: More premium income to receive is worth more to the seller.
A costlier protection leg (e.g. spreads have widened) hurts the seller.

intuition: Seller's value = premiums in minus protection out; positive when spreads have narrowed since inception.

name: CDS price with a fixed coupon (up-front payment)
prompt: With standardised fixed coupons, how is the quoted CDS price (per 100 notional) found from the CDS duration, its spread and the fixed coupon?

variables.meaning: CDS price per 100 of notional; 100 minus price is the buyer's up-front payment
duration of the CDS
CDS spread (decimal)
fixed coupon (decimal), e.g. 0.01 for 100 bps

corruptions.why: When the spread exceeds the coupon the price must fall below 100 so the buyer pays up front; adding the term moves the price the wrong way.
The annual spread gap must be multiplied by the CDS duration to value it over the life of the contract.
Only the gap between the spread and the fixed coupon is settled up front; the coupon itself is still paid running.

sensitivities.why: A wider spread than the coupon makes protection worth more than the coupon pays for, so the price falls.
A higher fixed coupon means the buyer pays more over time, so less is due up front and the price rises.
Lowers the price when s > c, raises it when s < c, no effect when s = c.

intuition: Spread above the fixed coupon: the buyer is underpaying each year, so pays duration x (s - c) up front.

name: Excess spread in a securitization
prompt: In a three-tiered securitization, how is the excess spread for year t computed?

variables.meaning: excess spread at the end of year t
aggregate loan interest received by the trust at the end of year t
bond coupon interest due to the junior (mezzanine) and senior bonds, a constant

corruptions.why: Excess spread is collateral interest in minus bond coupons out; this has the sign backwards.
The cap K limits what is diverted to the OC account; it is not deducted in computing excess spread.

sensitivities.why: More loan interest collected leaves more after paying bondholders.
Higher bond coupons due absorb more of the collateral interest.

intuition: What the loans pay in, minus what the senior and mezzanine bonds are owed; defaults shrink B_t but B stays fixed.

name: Annual diversion to the overcollateralization account
prompt: How much of the year's excess spread is diverted to the overcollateralization account, given the annual cap?

variables.meaning: amount of excess spread diverted to the OC account in year t
excess spread at the end of year t, B_t - B
maximum amount divertible annually (in the example $1,750,000)

corruptions.why: Swapping min and max makes the result always equal K (min(excess spread, 0) is never above 0), whatever the excess spread; the cap must be the outer min and the zero floor the inner max.
Without the cap K all positive excess spread would be diverted and equity would never receive anything.
Without the zero floor a negative excess spread would appear as a negative diversion; the shortfall is instead drawn from the account.

sensitivities.why: Raises the diversion only while excess spread is between 0 and K; above K the diversion is capped, below 0 it is zero.
Raises the diversion only if excess spread exceeds K.

intuition: Positive excess spread goes to the OC account up to the cap K; only the part above K reaches equity.

name: Overcollateralization account balance roll-forward
prompt: How is the overcollateralization account balance at the end of year t built from last year's balance, the money market rate, this year's diversion and recoveries?

variables.meaning: balance of the overcollateralization account at the end of year t
balance at the end of the previous year
money market rate earned on the account (decimal)
excess spread diverted into the account in year t
recoveries on loans defaulting in year t, paid into the account

corruptions.why: The existing balance earns the money market rate, so it grows by (1 + r).
Recoveries on defaulted loans are paid into the OC account, not through the waterfall.
Only the capped diversion OC_t goes to the account; excess spread above K goes to equity.

sensitivities.why: A bigger opening balance carries forward, plus interest.
A higher money market rate grows the balance faster (given a positive opening balance).
More diversion adds directly to the account.
Recoveries are paid into the account.

intuition: Last year's pot grows at the money market rate, then add this year's capped diversion and the recoveries.

name: Book-to-market ratio
prompt: How is the book-to-market ratio used to sort value from growth stocks computed from the balance sheet and the share price?
latex: \text{Book-to-market ratio} = \frac{\text{book value of equity}}{\text{market capitalisation}} = \frac{\text{total assets} - \text{total liabilities}}{\text{share price} \times \text{shares outstanding}}

variables.meaning: book value divided by market value of equity; high = value stock, low = growth stock
total assets minus total liabilities
share price times shares outstanding
balance-sheet total assets
balance-sheet total liabilities
market price per share
number of shares outstanding

corruptions.why: That is book value per share, a currency amount; without price in the denominator there is no ratio (the source-notes trap).
That is price-to-book; book-to-market puts book value on top, so high values mean cheap (value) stocks.
Book equity is assets minus liabilities, not total assets.

sensitivities.why: A falling price with unchanged book value raises the ratio, which is how falling stocks become value stocks.
More assets (liabilities fixed) means more book equity.
More liabilities reduce book equity.
More shares at the same price raise market cap relative to book.

intuition: Book on top, market below: a high number means you pay little for each dollar of book, which is a value stock.

name: Fama-French three-factor model
prompt: In the Fama-French (1993) model, what is an asset's expected return in terms of the risk-free rate and its loadings on the market, size and value factors?

variables.meaning: expected return on asset i
risk-free rate
asset's loading on the market factor
market risk premium
asset's loading on the size factor
risk premium of SMB: small minus big stocks by market capitalisation
asset's loading on the value factor
risk premium of HML: high minus low book-to-market stocks

corruptions.why: The market loading multiplies the market excess return, E(r_m - r_f), not the raw market return.
The factor premia are excess returns; the risk-free rate must be added back to get the total expected return.
Adding momentum (WML) gives Carhart's four-factor model, not the Fama-French three-factor model.

sensitivities.why: Holding the factor premia fixed, the expected return rises one-for-one with the risk-free rate.
Raises E(r_i) if the size loading is positive (small-cap tilt), lowers it if negative.
Raises E(r_i) if the value loading is positive, lowers it if negative (growth tilt).
With a positive market premium, more market exposure means a higher expected return.

intuition: CAPM plus two long-short tilts: small minus big (size) and high minus low book-to-market (value).
